title: The tools that read a binary for you
objective: By the end of this lesson you can disassemble a binary three different ways, list what a stripped binary still tells you, and drive a debugger to inspect registers, memory and the call stack of a running program.

blocks.text: Everything so far has used compiler output, where names and structure are still present. Real analysis usually starts from a finished binary. These are the tools for that, and the first thing they show is how much survives and how much does not.
objdump: what is actually in the file

blocks.caption: Real output, including the machine-code bytes
lines: /* Six instructions occupying 1, 3, 3, 2, 1 and 1 bytes. That variability
is the CISC encoding the architecture course described, made concrete:
RISC-V would have used exactly 4 bytes for every one of them. The nop
at the end is padding so the next function starts on an aligned address. */

blocks.title: The byte column is worth reading, not skipping
blocks.text: It shows the instruction lengths, which is how you know whether a jump target lands on a real instruction boundary. It also lets you spot data that the disassembler has mistaken for code: a run of bytes that decodes into nonsense mnemonics is usually a string table or a jump table being read as instructions. On a variable-length architecture a disassembler that starts at the wrong offset produces a completely different and completely plausible-looking instruction stream, so knowing where the boundaries really are matters.
What stripping removes, and what it cannot

blocks.caption: The same program before and after strip
lines: The same function, disassembled after stripping:
/* Byte for byte identical code. What was lost is only the names. This is
the difference between reading a binary that ships with symbols and one
that does not, and it is the whole reason reverse engineering is work:
the behaviour is fully visible, and the intent is not. */

rows: All the code, byte for byte
Dynamically linked function names, in the import table
The structure of calls and jumps
Any hint of the original source layout
Data layout, readable from address arithmetic

blocks.text: The third row on the left is often the most valuable: a stripped binary that calls into libc still has to name the functions it imports, so a list of imports tells you a great deal about what the program does. A binary importing socket, connect and send is doing networking whether or not any of its own functions have names.
A first pass over an unfamiliar binary

blocks.caption: Four commands, in this order
lines: file ./prog              # architecture, format, stripped or not, static or dynamic
nm -g ./prog             # global symbols, if any survived
strings -a ./prog        # embedded text: messages, paths, URLs, format strings
readelf -h ./prog        # ELF header: entry point, type
readelf -d ./prog        # dynamic section: which libraries it needs
objdump -T ./prog        # dynamic symbols: what it imports
/* Run them in that order because each narrows the next. strings before
objdump in particular: a format string like "user %s logged in" tells
you what a function does faster than reading its instructions. */

blocks.caption: Real output from gdb and lldb on the same binary
lines: Dump of assembler code for function add3:
/* The same six instructions from three tools. Note the offsets <+0>, <+1>,
<+4> -- both debuggers number instructions by their byte offset from the
function's start, which is often more useful than the absolute address
because it does not change when the program is loaded somewhere else. */

blocks.text: Both default to AT&T. The gdb output above is Intel only because the command set the flavour explicitly; the lldb output beside it was left at its default and came out AT&T, which is why the two look different despite describing identical bytes. This is the difference the syntax lesson prepared you for, and it is why the first command in the gdb line sets the flavour explicitly.

blocks.caption: The commands that matter, in both debuggers
lines: break at a function         break add3                   b add3
break at an address         break *0x100000344           b -a 0x100000344
one INSTRUCTION forward     stepi                        thread step-inst
one source line forward     step                         thread step-in
read registers              info registers rdi rsi       register read rdi rsi
read memory as 8-byte hex   x/4xg $rsp                   memory read -f x -s8 -c4 $rsp
read memory as a string     x/s $rdi                     memory read -f s $rdi
watch a memory location     watch *0x1234                watchpoint set expression -- 0x1234
/* stepi is the one that separates debugging source from debugging machine
code. step follows source lines and will walk through a whole optimised
loop in one keystroke; stepi advances exactly one instruction, which is
what you want when the source line no longer corresponds to anything. */

blocks.title: x/4xg $rsp is the single most useful command
blocks.text: It prints the four 8-byte values at the top of the stack. Immediately after entering a function you will see the return address there; inside a frame you will see saved registers and locals. Learning to read that output against the frame layout from the stack-frames lesson is what turns a debugger from a stepping tool into an inspection tool. The letters are: x for hexadecimal, g for giant, meaning 8 bytes.

blocks.title: A debugger needs permission to attach
blocks.text: On macOS, debugging a binary you did not build may require it to be signed with the get-task-allow entitlement, and emulated binaries may not be debuggable at all. On Linux, ptrace_scope may prevent attaching to a process you did not start. If a debugger refuses to run or attach, check the platform's restriction before assuming the binary is doing something clever to resist you — it usually is not.

blocks.title: Analyse a binary you did not build
steps: Compile a small program with several functions, then copy it and strip the copy
Run file, nm and strings on both and record what differs
Disassemble one function in both and confirm the bytes are identical
Set a breakpoint on a function, run, and print the first three argument registers
Print the top four values on the stack and identify the return address
Use stepi to advance through the prologue one instruction at a time, watching rsp
Take a backtrace and match it against the frames you have been watching
Pick any system binary on your machine and do a first pass with the four commands
blocks.expected: Identical code from both copies, argument registers holding the values you passed, and a stack whose top word is the return address into the caller. The final step is where this becomes a skill rather than an exercise: running the four-command pass on a real binary and forming an accurate impression of what it does within a minute or two is the everyday reality of the work.

cheatsheet: objdump -d shows addresses, machine-code bytes and instructions
The byte column reveals instruction lengths and misdecoded data
Instruction lengths measured here: 1, 3, 3, 2, 1, 1 bytes for six instructions
Stripping removes names but not code, strings, imports or structure
First pass: file, nm -g, strings -a, objdump -d — in that order
On Linux add readelf -h, readelf -d and objdump -T
gdb and lldb both default to AT&T — set the flavour explicitly rather than assuming
Both number instructions as <+n>, the byte offset from the function start
stepi advances one instruction; step advances one source line
x/4xg $rsp prints the top four 8-byte stack values; x is hex, g is 8 bytes
A debugger that cannot attach is usually blocked by the platform, not by the binary

checkpoint.prompt: Why is the machine-code byte column in objdump output worth reading?

choices.A: It is needed to patch the binary
choices.B: It shows the instruction encodings for reference

checkpoint.explanation: You can tell whether a jump target lands on a real boundary and whether data is being misdecoded as code. On a variable-length architecture, starting a disassembly at the wrong offset produces a completely different and completely plausible instruction stream. Knowing where the boundaries are is what prevents that.

checkpoint.prompt: A binary has been stripped. What can you still learn about it?

choices.C: All the code, all string constants, the names of dynamically imported functions, and the data layout readable from address arithmetic

checkpoint.explanation: Stripping removes names, not behaviour. The import list is often the most informative part: a binary importing socket, connect and send is doing networking regardless of what its own functions are called.

checkpoint.prompt: You are stopped inside an optimised function whose source line no longer corresponds to anything. Which command do you want?

choices.D: stepi, which advances exactly one machine instruction

checkpoint.explanation: step follows source lines and can walk an entire optimised loop in one keystroke. stepi is the command for debugging machine code rather than source.

checkpoint.prompt: You have just stopped at the first instruction of a function. What does x/4xg $rsp show you?

choices.B: The top four 8-byte stack values, the first of which is the return address pushed by call

checkpoint.explanation: Reading that output against the frame layout is what turns a debugger into an inspection tool. x is hexadecimal and g means giant, eight bytes.
